options: Yes, goes back alone or pushed back

red_flags: Dizziness, collapse, tachycardia, or postural drop with bleeding — hemodynamically significant hemorrhage; urgent surgical referral
Age over 45 with new bleeding plus altered habit, weight loss, or tenesmus — colorectal carcinoma until excluded
Iron-deficiency anemia with rectal bleeding at any age — the source must be found, not assumed to be piles
Melena or blood mixed through the stool — proximal source, not an anal one
Bloody diarrhea with fever, distension, and toxicity — severe colitis
exam: Record BP and pulse, sitting and standing — postural drop grades the bleed
Look for pallor of conjunctiva and palmar creases
Palpate the abdomen for a mass (left or right iliac fossa) and for hepatomegaly
Perform a digital rectal exam — a palpable rectal mass, blood on the glove, or melena each redirect the whole pathway
Inspect the anal margin — fissure, prolapsed or thrombosed piles
Proctoscopy — bleeding internal hemorrhoids seen directly
Percuss for distension and listen to bowel sounds when colitis is suspected
Palpate the left supraclavicular fossa for a hard node
Record temperature — fever supports infective or inflammatory colitis over the anatomical causes

investigations.why: Microcytic anemia supports carcinoma, angiodysplasia, or chronic colitis; a normal count with typical outlet bleeding fits hemorrhoids or fissure; acute drop grades a brisk bleed
Trophozoites rule in amebic dysentery — a common Iraqi cause of bloody diarrhea — and culture separates infective colitis from ulcerative colitis
Raised values support active colitis (ulcerative or infective) over hemorrhoids, fissure, polyps, and angiodysplasia
A urea rise out of proportion to creatinine supports a proximal (upper GI) source presenting as dark rectal bleeding
Anticoagulant use or liver disease can turn any of the listed sources into a major bleed and must be quantified
Directly confirms an anorectal source — hemorrhoids, fissure, a low rectal tumor — before blaming piles
Second-line — mandatory if over 45 with new bleeding, anemia, altered habit, family history, or no anorectal source found: the definitive test for carcinoma, polyps, colitis, and angiodysplasia
Second-line — if melena or a disproportionate urea rise points to a bleeding source above the colon
